questions.q: What makes the Bellwood Apparel case study materially different from Lessons 1-4?
options: It is the only case study involving Salesforce at all
Data flows in both directions between the same two systems on the same records, rather than one-way or on clearly separated fields
It is the only case study that doesn't involve any customer or lead data
Bellwood Apparel does not use a marketing platform of any kind
questions.explain: Lessons 1-4 each involved either one-way data flow or two systems owning clearly separate fields. Bellwood's case is the first where both systems can originate changes to the very same shared records, which introduces the update-loop problem.

questions.q: How does an update loop actually happen in a naive bidirectional sync, per this lesson?
options: A record is deleted in both systems simultaneously, causing a conflict error

A change pushed from one system is seen by the other system's sync logic as a new change and pushed right back, and the cycle repeats indefinitely, burning API calls and potentially re-triggering automation each time
Two different sales reps edit the same contact record in Salesforce at the same time
The marketing platform refuses to accept any data from Salesforce
questions.explain: A loop happens when each system's sync treats an incoming change (that it itself caused) as new, pushing it back to the other system, which pushes it back again -- repeating indefinitely and potentially re-triggering downstream automation on every bounce.

questions.q: Which update-loop prevention technique does this lesson say Bellwood's design uses, and why?
options: Field-level change detection with a cooldown, because it's the only technique that technically works
A source-system tag marking which system originated a change, chosen because it's simpler to reason about and catches the loop at its root cause
Disabling the sync entirely whenever any field changes
Randomly delaying every sync job by several hours
questions.explain: The lesson describes two valid techniques -- a source-system tag and field-level change detection with a cooldown -- and states Bellwood's design uses the source-system tag specifically because it's simpler to reason about and addresses the loop's root cause.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat suppression/consent status as integration-critical data rather than a secondary marketing concern?
options: Because suppression status never actually changes once set
Because a sales rep working a lead who has legally opted out of marketing contact, with no record of it in Salesforce, is a real compliance exposure
Because marketing platforms are legally required to delete suppressed contacts within 24 hours
Because suppression status is not technically possible to sync between systems
questions.explain: An opt-out that never reaches Salesforce creates a real compliance exposure if a rep contacts someone who has withdrawn consent -- which is why the lesson holds this field to the same reliability bar as core identity data, not a lower one.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens if an integration team never explicitly decides a matching strategy for records from both systems?
options: The integration simply refuses to run at all until a decision is made
There is no matching behavior of any kind, and every record is treated as unique forever
Whatever the underlying tools happen to do by default becomes the de facto policy, usually without anyone having actually chosen it
Salesforce automatically merges all similar-looking records without any review
questions.explain: Leaving the matching strategy undecided doesn't mean nothing happens -- it means the tools' default behavior quietly becomes the real policy, which is why the lesson frames matching strategy as a deliberate design decision rather than something to leave implicit.
